recommendation.what_this_means: Returns is the strongest opportunity area: 83 records describe a decision stalling on it, and only 21 describe resolving it (20% resolution rate). An independently clustered theme corroborates it — “Positive Return and Exchange Experiences” (Resolve, n=52). 179 records describe leaving the platform to resolve it, so the uncertainty is currently answered off-app or not at all. questions.question: Why do users add fashion products to their wishlist?
questions.answer: The corpus surfaces exactly one save-motivation with direct evidence: PRICE WATCHING. Theme full:38 records users who wishlist an item specifically to track its price, then report the price RISING after they save it. flagged:23 shows discounts/coupons as the event users wait for. No other save motivation (inspiration, comparison shortlist, bookmarking) appears at measurable volume.

questions.caveat: Under-powered. Only 283 community records (2.1% of corpus); the other 97.9% are store reviews, which do not carry save-motivation narratives. Treat price-watch as the one evidenced motive, not as the dominant one.

questions.question: What prevents wishlisted products from eventually being purchased?
questions.answer: Three evidenced blockers, all at the price/checkout end rather than the product-doubt end: (1) price increases after saving (full:38); (2) price judged too high vs alternatives (full:18); (3) fees added at checkout — COD, platform and delivery charges (full:25). The engine's own opportunity scoring instead ranks RETURNS uncertainty highest (83 stalled vs 21 resolved, 20% resolution rate), driven by records where return/exchange risk is what keeps the decision open.

questions.question: What uncertainties remain after users have identified a product they like?
questions.answer: Ranked by unresolved stall volume: Returns/exchange risk (83 stalled, 20% resolved) far ahead of Quality (10, 44%), Colour accuracy (5, 58%), Size (4, 73%) and Fit (2, 75%). The pattern is that fit and size doubts largely DO get resolved once users engage, while return-policy risk stays open — users are unsure what happens if the item is wrong, and that keeps the decision suspended.

questions.question: What causes users to postpone a purchase?
questions.answer: Waiting for a sale or discount is the clearest postponement trigger (flagged:23, full:18). full:38 shows the perverse counterpart: users who postpone to watch a price then find it has risen, which converts postponement into abandonment rather than a later purchase.

questions.question: How do users compare multiple shortlisted products?
questions.answer: No theme in this corpus describes side-by-side comparison of shortlisted items. Store reviews concern a single transaction and structurally cannot show comparison behaviour, and the 283 community records did not yield a comparison cluster. This question needs the primary research interviews or a substantially larger Reddit corpus.

questions.question: What information do users seek outside the app before purchasing?
questions.answer: 179 records reference an external source while touching an uncertainty axis — the single strongest externalisation signal in the run, and the reason Returns scores as the top opportunity. Community themes full:13 (users asking others for budget/quality/sizing recommendations) and full:12 (outfit/fit-check posts sourcing and socially validating items) show the behaviour directly: users leave the product surface and ask people.

questions.question: What role do fit, size, styling, price, reviews, occasion and social validation play?
questions.answer: Measured as stalled-vs-resolved per axis: Returns 83/21 (20% resolved) dominates. Price 13/18 (58%) and Styling 2/12 (86%) resolve readily. Size 4/11 (73%) and Fit 2/6 (75%) resolve more often than they stall — notable, because fit is the assumed fashion blocker and this corpus does not support that assumption. Social validation is barely present (1/2). Occasion 2/6.

questions.question: When do users use the wishlist as genuine purchase intent versus simply as a bookmarking mechanism?
questions.answer: The corpus cannot separate these. full:38 evidences one specific use — the wishlist as a price-watch instrument — which is intent-adjacent but conditional. Nothing distinguishes a genuine-intent save from a bookmarking save, because neither store reviews nor the available community records narrate the save decision itself.

questions.caveat: This is the question the brief most directly poses and the corpus most clearly cannot answer. It should drive the interview guide.

questions.question: How do these behaviours differ across user segments?
questions.answer: No segmentation is possible from this data. The corpus carries no demographic, tenure or basket-value attributes, and the only available split — by app — is a platform split, not a user segment. Per-app theme skew exists (Nykaa Fashion dominates full:1, AJIO full:7) but reflects each app's service performance, not user type.
questions.caveat: Requires primary research. Segment choice for Part 3 cannot be evidenced from this engine alone.

questions.question: What unmet needs emerge consistently across user conversations?
questions.answer: One need recurs with the strongest evidence in the run: certainty about return/exchange terms BEFORE committing (83 stalled, 20% resolved, and the largest externalisation signal). A second, narrower but sharply evidenced need is price stability on saved items — users experience wishlisting as something that works against them (full:38).

source_disclosure.corpus: 13,552 usable records: 12,237 Play, 1,032 App Store, 283 Reddit.
source_disclosure.weighting: Community/discussion text is the intended quantified base but is only 2.1% of this corpus. Headline percentages against the primary denominator are therefore under-powered and are reported as such.
source_disclosure.sources_dropped: YouTube dropped at the sample gate (0.1% hit-rate, n=1,660). X/Twitter never sampled.
source_disclosure.primary_research: Not yet conducted. triangulation.json is intentionally absent.

gate_distribution.note: Themes concentrate at Resolve (12) and Other-unrelated (14). The large Other-unrelated share is the store corpus asserting itself: post-purchase delivery and refund failures are not wishlist-funnel events.

corroboration.note: Community and discussion text (Reddit, YouTube comments, forums) is the primary corpus for this engine — it is where users narrate their own purchase deliberation. App and Play Store reviews are retained as a secondary corroboration corpus: they are written at moments of transactional friction and structurally under-represent the reasoning behind an unpurchased saved item.
corroboration.verdict: 9 of 31 themes (29%) appear in BOTH the community corpus and the store-review corpus. Cross-source themes are the most defensible findings in this run; single-source themes are reported with that limitation stated.
